events.name: ‘United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today’ ADST Traveling Exhibition
events.description: UNC Global Affairs is pleased to partner with the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training (ADST) to host a traveling exhibition on the history of American diplomacy, “United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today.” Created with support from the Una Chapman Cox Foundation, the 21-panel exhibition celebrates diplomatic accomplishments and traces diplomacy’s role across America’s 250-year history, from Benjamin Franklin’s mission to Paris during the Revolutionary War, to 21st-century challenges such as transnational terrorism, climate change and global health. The exhibition begins during the opening reception for Diplomacy Week 2026 on Monday, Sept. 28, and will be on display in the FedEx Global Education Center until Friday, Oct. 2. Read more about the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training Founded in 1986, ADST is a nonprofit, nonpartisan, 501(c)3 educational organization that has conducted and posted more than 2,500 transcripts of oral history interviews of former diplomats on its website — the world’s largest diplomatic oral history collection. ADST’s collection is a unique and priceless historical record of post-World War II U.S. diplomacy, praised by scholars, educators and diplomatic practitioners alike. ADST is committed to strengthening public appreciation of diplomacy’s contribution to America’s national interests, and enriching the professional knowledge of diplomatic practitioners. - - - This event is a part of Diplomacy Week 2026! Diplomacy Week offers students and, on a couple occasions, members of the community, opportunities to engage closely with experts whose work has shaped U.S. foreign policy. Explore other events on the UNC Global Affairs website and join us in celebrating 250 years of American diplomacy!

events.name: DICE Book Launch and Discussion: Sick Work
events.venue: Rubenstein Library Holsti-Anderson Family Assembly Room 153
events.description: Please join the Disability Inclusion and Community Empowerment (DICE) Affinity Group, Duke University Press, and the Department of Cultural Anthropology for the book launch of "Sick Work: Exhaustion, Labor, and Invisible Illness" by Dr. Emily Lim Rogers, Assistant Professor of Cultural Anthropology. This event is being held in recognition of National Disability Employment Awareness Month, and Dr. Rogers will be in conversation with Dr. Catherine Clune-Taylor, Assistant Professor of Gender, Sexuality, and Feminist Studies. From the book jacket: In "Sick Work," Emily Lim Rogers shows the unpaid labor it takes to be recognized as sick in the United States. Through a historical and ethnographic account of myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS)-a disease defined by disproportionate exhaustion after any form of exertion, which has no cure or treatment-she reveals how changing formations of labor decide what counts as disability and what does not. Sickness, she writes, is not work's opposite. Rather, the frequent dismissal of their disease leaves people with ME/CFS to do their own labor of disease advocacy, or "sick work," even as their symptoms prevent many from working paid jobs. Rogers presents a history of the discursive construction of chronic fatigue and demonstrates its development alongside capitalism since the dawn of industrial management science in the late nineteenth century. These histories, she argues, echo through to the present day, shaping the denial of ME/CFS and the stigma that surrounds it. Examining the everyday lives of people with ME/CFS and their activist movements, "Sick Work" describes how they swim upstream against strong tides of disbelief and demands a radical transformation of how work is defined and valued. This hybrid event will take place in-person and on Zoom. Accessible parking and building information can be found on the Libraries' website, and a selection of DICE-branded swag will be available for free. Human-assisted live captioning through Ava will be provided, while any additional accommodation requests should be directed to Access and Accommodation Services. Members of the Duke community can check out the book online through the Duke University Libraries, and the Gothic Bookshop will be on-site selling physical copies for signing. Please register online to help us estimate attendance. For any questions, contact DukeDICE@duke.edu.

events.name: Worlds of 1776: “The American Constitution: A Thousand-Year History?”
events.venue: Smith Warehouse, Ahmadieh Family Lecture Hall, Bay 4, C105
events.description: Join us for conversation with Professor Mark Peterson (Yale) about his new book The Making and Breaking of the American Constitution: A Thousand Year History. This book charts the history and aims of the American constitution from its origins in an agrarian past to the grave crisis we face today. Peterson traces the American constitutional tradition to the control of land in medieval England, showing how the founders incorporated the aspirations of Magna Carta with the administrative principles of the Domesday Book, a meticulous survey and valuation of landed property commissioned by William the Conqueror. This framework encouraged the growth of democratic self-government but also institutionalized the colonization of territory and the expulsion of Indigenous peoples, establishing a legal blueprint for transforming tribal lands into revenue-yielding real estate for settlers. Peterson's riveting narrative paints an arresting picture of a dynamic republic whose frame of government has changed enormously to meet the challenges of the modern age but whose written constitution has changed very little. Marking the 250th anniversary of American independence, The Making and Breaking of the American Constitution reveals how this widening disconnect threatens the very existence of our democracy. It calls for a constitution that sustains the ideals developed over the past thousand years while meeting the challenges of the future. Mark Peterson joined the Yale history faculty in 2018. He earned his Ph.D. in History at Harvard University and previously taught at the University of Iowa (1998-2007) and the University of California, Berkeley (2007-2018), where he served as chair of the History Department. He is also the author of The City-State of Boston: The Rise and Fall of an Atlantic Power, 1630-1865 (Princeton, 2019), and The Price of Redemption: The Spiritual Economy of Puritan New England (Stanford, 1997). He is now at work on Revolution's Ends: A History of the American Revolution for the 21st Century, designed to connect the war and political transformations of the late 18th century to the explosive growth in settler population, territorial expansion, and consumption patterns that characterized this world-transforming era. This event is part of the "Worlds of 1776" series, co-sponsored by the Department of History, the John Hope Franklin Humanities Institute, and the Bass Connections "Worlds of 1776" research team.

events.name: Fluid Master
events.description: Can an oil change be filmed as a fluid master? Join artist Kenya (Robinson) for a free public event exploring the surprising connections between documentary filmmaking and auto mechanics through a live, embodied performance. In filmmaking, a "fluid master" is an entire scene captured in one continuous shot while the camera remains in motion. For this event, Kenya will perform two live oil changes as continuous fluid master shots, inviting participants to consider how routine automotive maintenance can be transformed through the language of filmmaking. As she works, Kenya will engage attendees in a conversation about her life and practice as a Black woman, fine artist, and mechanic. Come view the action from multiple camera angles, including a live GoPro feed, while taking part in an artist talk that explores labor, performance, observation, and the stories embedded in everyday systems. The event will take place in the Center for Documentary Studies parking lot and includes refreshments and beverages. Space is limited to 25 - 30 people, so please register to reserve your spot here: https://rsvp.duke.edu/event/f23fe0fa-ab31-482e-895f-d11d694f0b89/summary The promotional image is from TURBO TAROT, Kenya's new artist-directed project that uses generative AI as one component of an iterative visualization and production process. Kenya developed the project's conceptual framework, automotive-to-tarot correspondences, visual system, imagery, and individual card concepts, using AI tools as one component of the artistic process. Interested in exploring the ideas behind TURBO TAROT? Join Kenya for a second free public event on October 3 at 10 am at CDS, where she will explore automotive systems through the symbolic framework of the tarot, blending automotive knowledge, philosophy, and live tarot readings.

events.name: Katherine Dunham, Holistic Practice: Dance Education and Activism Community Conversation and Panel
events.description: We invite you to a community conversation with April Berry to bring together your experience in the master class and film screening. The discussion invites conversation about the Dunham class process and the importance of the Magic of Katherine Dunham and Ms. Dunham's multidimensional work as a choreographer, teacher, writer, anthropologist, and cultural activist. Triangle Area dance educator panelists will share their unique perspectives on diverse dance planning, pedagogy and community building with arts education and activism. April Berry brings to the conversation her knowledge of and experience with Dunham's pedagogical approaches to holistic education, the Dunham Technique as it developed from Katherine Dunham's choreography, community activism, and socialization through the arts and practices that have emerged in relation to Ms. Dunham's innovative, foundational work, which is vital and impactful as a community-building and transformational force. 6:15-7:45 - Katherine Dunham, Holistic Practice: Dance Education and Activism Community Conversation and Panel, Rubenstein Arts Center 202 Panel Moderator - Andrea E. Woods Valdes, Duke Dance Program Panel: April Berry; Nile Russell, American Dance Festival Director of Education; Kristi Vincent Johnson, North Carolina Central University Dance Director; Carol Finley, Meredith College Chair; Keisha Gee, Elon University; Robin Gee, University of North Carolina Greensboro, Director of Graduate Studies; J. Lorand Matory, Duke University Distinguished Professor of Cultural Anthropology. 7:45 - Reception to follow in the Ruby Lounge Open to the public, all are welcome. Please sign up: https://duke.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_4NMt9PUGsMngb6m Free parking is available. Campus Drive lot via Anderson Street. This residency was made possible by the Hymowitz Guest Artist Fund.

events.name: Screen/Society--"Sherman's March" (Ross McElwee, 1986) | new 4K restoration
events.description: Film Screening: "Sherman's March" (Ross McElwee, 1986, 158 min, USA, DCP) Armed with a 16mm camera and a grant to make a documentary about the lingering aftermath of William Tecumseh Sherman's 1864 march to the sea, Ross McElwee gets sidetracked. After his girlfriend breaks up with him, Ross shifts his attention from the historical to the personal, to the battlefield of modern love, and embarks on a sociological chronicle that documents the courting rites and rituals of the New South. A generous and humanistic portrait of several remarkable women that Ross meets along the way, "Sherman's March" sketches its characters with novelistic sensitivity: Pat, an aspiring actress with a yen for Burt Reynolds; Claudia, a roller-skating interior designer; Jackie, the activist whose anti-nuclear advocacy dovetails with Ross's deepest fears; and above all, Charleen Swansea, Ross's mentor and a one-woman Greek chorus of unsolicited romantic counsel. A landmark of first-person filmmaking that presaged everything from Michael Moore to reality TV, "Sherman's March" is now available in a new 4K restoration - just in time for its 40th anniversary. -- World Premiere - Berlin International Film Festival, 1986 -- Grand Jury Prize, US Premiere - Sundance Film Festival, 1987 -- National Society of Film Critics Award - 1987 -- U.S. National Film Registry, Library of Congress - 2000 -- "One of the Top 20 Documentaries of All Time" - International Documentary Association

events.name: ‘United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today’ ADST Traveling Exhibition
events.description: UNC Global Affairs is pleased to partner with the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training (ADST) to host a traveling exhibition on the history of American diplomacy, “United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today.” Created with support from the Una Chapman Cox Foundation, the 21-panel exhibition celebrates diplomatic accomplishments and traces diplomacy’s role across America’s 250-year history, from Benjamin Franklin’s mission to Paris during the Revolutionary War, to 21st-century challenges such as transnational terrorism, climate change and global health. The exhibition begins during the opening reception for Diplomacy Week 2026 on Monday, Sept. 28, and will be on display in the FedEx Global Education Center until Friday, Oct. 2. Read more about the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training Founded in 1986, ADST is a nonprofit, nonpartisan, 501(c)3 educational organization that has conducted and posted more than 2,500 transcripts of oral history interviews of former diplomats on its website — the world’s largest diplomatic oral history collection. ADST’s collection is a unique and priceless historical record of post-World War II U.S. diplomacy, praised by scholars, educators and diplomatic practitioners alike. ADST is committed to strengthening public appreciation of diplomacy’s contribution to America’s national interests, and enriching the professional knowledge of diplomatic practitioners. - - - This event is a part of Diplomacy Week 2026! Diplomacy Week offers students and, on a couple occasions, members of the community, opportunities to engage closely with experts whose work has shaped U.S. foreign policy. Explore other events on the UNC Global Affairs website and join us in celebrating 250 years of American diplomacy!

events.name: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
events.address: 121 E. Cameron Avenue, Chapel Hill, NC
events.description: Art and Art History Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering August 20-October 15, 2026 Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026. Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University. Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University. Admission: Free Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE. For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

events.name: Philosophical Approaches to Speech and Expression
events.description: How does philosophy conceptualize academic freedom? How can philosophical discourse shed light on our animating questions of freedom in teaching and research? Please join NC State and Duke universities for a conversation with Richard Amesbury of Arizona State University, Ásta Kristjana Sveinsdóttir of Duke University and Anton Ford of the University of Chicago. This event is part of Sharing Ground, a joint NC State–Duke seminar exploring how the humanities can deepen our understanding of academic freedom and the university’s role in sustaining democratic life. Bringing together scholars, students and academic leaders, the seminar asks how humanistic inquiry can foster principled disagreement and a more vibrant culture of free inquiry on campus.

events.name: Olds Elementary School History Harvest
events.description: Fred A. Olds Elementary School will celebrate its centennial in 2027. NC State public history faculty member and Olds Elementary parent Alicia Ebbitt McGill is co-leading partnerships between Olds Elementary, the NC State Department of History, the University Libraries Special Collections Research Center at NC State and the Raleigh Historic Resources and Museums Program to: Research the history of Olds ElementaryConnect with the school's alumniOrganize the school's historic archivesDevelop educational resources, including an exhibit about the school's historyOn Oct. 3 from 9 a.m. to noon, the Olds Centennial Programming Committee will host History Harvest at the school to connect with alumni, collect historical documents, get input from stakeholders about the exhibit and programming and spread the word about the April 2027 centennial celebration. At this event, we will scan and document historical materials that people bring and have hands-on activities, including a historical timeline and postcard project for people to share their memories of Olds Elementary. Please bring any historical memorabilia you have of Olds Elementary and come share your memories of the school. Ainsley Powell, curator of collections for the Raleigh Museum, will be at the event to answer questions about the kinds of materials the museum collects and best practices for preserving your own personal collections. If you can't attend History Harvest but have a connection to Olds Elementary, fill out the database form to share your experiences and learn more about the centennial programming. If you have questions, contact McGill at 412-398-6447, Allison Ottley at 703-727-4016 or send an email to oldscentennial@gmail.com.

events.name: Vintage Base Ball Day at the DAP
events.description: A day of vintage base ball played at the Historic Durham Athletic Park ! ***Any tickets purchased for our 2025 Vintage Base Ball event are valid for 2026!*** The iconic Durham Athletic Park has hosted baseball games since 1926 and was even featured in an iconic baseball film, but Durham’s baseball roots are even deeper. The first century of baseball was marked by racial segregation and separate leagues for black and white athletes at the DAP until the 1950s; however, Duke Homestead welcomes all people to participate and honors the struggles and achievements of the many players over the past century who brought us the Durham baseball culture we know today. Players will wear historic uniforms, follow historic gameplay, and use historic equipment. The games will follow 1860 and 1869 Beadles Rules. We invite you to connect with the history of this sport, this place, and this community by enjoying an afternoon out at the ball park. Admission to the game is $10; children under 4 years old will be admitted free. Game tickets can be purchased online through Eventbrite, or in person at the Duke Homestead visitor center, as well as at the gate on game day. Early-Bird tickets for $5 available until 9/21 (online here or at the Duke Homestead visitor center). Enjoy a family-friendly day at the ball park complete with “old fashioned” concessions, food, beer, and historic music. Spectators are encouraged to come dressed in your favorite historical, vintage, or retro inspired outfits. We believe in vintage style, not vintage values! Kids will get to play historic games with our costumed interpreters, as well as have the opportunity to run the bases in-between ball games. Joining our local Duke Homestead team this year will be The Shiners from Rockingham, VA and a special team from the Durham Fire Department! The first game will be played at 11am, with games at 12:30pm and 2pm to follow. This game is a fundraiser for the Duke Homestead State Historic Site and it is sponsored by the Duke Homestead Education and History Corporation (the site’s volunteer, non-profit support organization), Measurement, Inc., and Stone Brothers & Byrd. Free parking available at the lot at 412 Morris St, Durham, NC 27701. A couple of handicap spaces are available in the DAP parking lot. **We are unable to offer refunds on purchased tickets. All cancelled tickets will be considered a donation to the site and will be used for future educational programming.**

events.name: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
events.address: 121 E. Cameron Avenue, Chapel Hill, NC
events.description: Art and Art History Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering August 20-October 15, 2026 Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026. Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University. Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University. Admission: Free Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE. For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

events.name: An Afternoon with Dartmouth's Dr. Susannah Heschel, Eli Black Distinguished Professor of Jewish Studies
events.description: Is there a place for Jews and Jewish Studies at the American University? Universities are crucial to the strength and vitality of our country, and Jewish Studies has been foundational for shaping Jewish identity, culture, religion, and politics. Knowledge of Jewish history and thought is the foundation for understanding the meaning and responsibility of Jewish life. This lecture will trace the rise of the modern university in 19th century Europe and the enthusiastic participation by Jews in academic scholarship as well as the hostility they have encountered at crucial moments. Jewish scholars made extraordinary contributions to the academy, and the field of Jewish Studies changed our understanding of Western civilization. CLE credit is available.

events.name: Remembering & Resisting: LGBTQ+ History From Nazi Germany to Today
events.description: Visit the Gregg Museum of Art & Design for the opening of the exhibition Remembering & Resisting: LGBTQ+ History From Nazi Germany to Today and a keynote address by curator Jake Newsome, founder of The Pink Triangle Legacies Project. Newsome's keynote address, "Enemies of the State: The Nazi Persecution of LGBTQ+ People," will examine the complex motivations behind Nazi leaders' choice to persecute LGBTQ+ people and to present it as vital to the success of the Third Reich. A Q&A and a book signing will follow the presentation. Please register to attend. Remembering & Resisting: LGBTQ+ History From Nazi Germany to Today is a traveling exhibit that explores the persecution of queer and trans people under Nazi rule and the long, ongoing struggle to reclaim their histories. Beginning in Weimar Germany’s early LGBTQ+ movements, the exhibit traces how the Nazi regime targeted those deemed “undesirable” and how survivors faced continued criminalization and silence long after 1945. The exhibition will be on display at the Gregg Museum through Oct. 23.

events.name: Plant ID for the Home Gardener: Fall Edition
events.price: $200 for JC Raulston Arboretum members, $250 for nonmembers
events.description: How do you tell one plant from another when they look almost exactly alike? Is that a boxwood or a Japanese holly? Which features actually matter when you're trying to identify a plant? And what do all those botanical names really mean? Plant identification is both an art and a science, and understanding plant nomenclature, taxonomy and identification can make every gardener more knowledgeable and confident, helping you select the right plants for your landscape and better understand how to care for them. Bryce Lane, former host of In the Garden With Bryce Lane, will lead a five-week class that will explore the principles of plant identification. Rather than simply memorizing names, you'll learn how to look at a plant and understand what you're seeing. We'll examine leaves, stems, buds, flowers, fruits, branching patterns and other characteristics that can help you narrow down an identification, with particular attention to the trees, shrubs and herbaceous plants commonly encountered in the garden and landscape. We'll also explore how today's plant identification apps, digital keys and landscape planning tools can work alongside your knowledge to help you identify plants and determine where they might fit best. You can attend the course in person at the JC Raulston Arboretum or virtually. To learn more about the course and to register, visit the arboretum website.

events.name: Ackland Film Forum: "Set It Off" (F. Gary Gray, 1996)
events.venue: The Lumina Theater, 620 Market Street, Chapel Hill, 27516, United States
events.description: Jada Pinkett Smith, Queen Latifah, and Vivica A. Fox anchor this energetic reworking of the heist film. After a series of setbacks leaves four Black women with few viable paths forward, they embark on a string of increasingly audacious bank robberies. Blending humor, suspense, and tragedy, Set It Off captures both the bonds of friendship and the pressures of race, gender, and economic inequality in 1990s urban America. This film will be introduced by Professor Daelena Tinnin-Gadson, UNC-Chapel Hill Department of English and Comparative Literature. It will be screened at 7:30 p.m. at The Lumina Theater (620 Market St, Chapel Hill, NC 27516). Tickets are free for all audience members, and registration is required via The Lumina’s webpage. When this link is live, click to reserve your free ticket. UNC-Chapel Hill students can receive CLE credit for attending by scanning the QR code at the event. About the Series: Join the Ackland Film Forum this fall for Socially Charged Crime Thrillers: Snapshots of Social Anxiety, a series that accompanies the Ackland exhibition Care and Concern: Recent Acquisitions of Modern and Contemporary Art. As vehicles of social commentary and stylistic bravura, crime thrillers often register the pressures and contradictions of their historical moment. Across nearly half a century, the films in this series stage encounters with political power, public trust, inequality, and ambition through assassination plots, botched robberies, and media-driven spectacle. From the crises of the late 1960s to the intensified media environments of the twenty-first century, these works show how genre cinema can capture social anxiety in real time. Each film stands both as a gripping narrative and as a record of a world under strain, where institutions falter and everyday life becomes fraught with conflict. The Ackland Film Forum is co-organized by the Ackland Art Museum and UNC Film Studies, housed in the UNC-Chapel Hill Department of English and Comparative Literature.

events.name: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
events.address: 121 E. Cameron Avenue, Chapel Hill, NC
events.description: Art and Art History Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering August 20-October 15, 2026 Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026. Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University. Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University. Admission: Free Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE. For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

events.name: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
events.address: 121 E. Cameron Avenue, Chapel Hill, NC
events.description: Art and Art History Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering August 20-October 15, 2026 Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026. Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University. Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University. Admission: Free Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE. For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

events.name: Think and Do: The Future of Climate Solutions
events.description: Join the KIETS Climate Leaders Program on Oct. 7-8 for our 5th annual fall symposium, Think and Do: The Future of Climate Solutions. This two-day event brings together students, faculty, industry partners, leading experts and community members to highlight interdisciplinary collaboration and transform research into real-world impact. Together, we’ll explore the future of climate solutions across four core themes: Climate Science Data: Translating research, data and modeling into actionable strategies for resilienceInnovation and Entrepreneurship: Launching climate-tech ventures, piloting market-driven ideas, and exploring opportunitiesBuildings: Transforming green infrastructure, resilient design, and energy efficiency in the built environmentTextiles: Reimagining circular fashion, bio-based materials and sustainable manufacturing processesThe symposium’s sponsor is the Climate and Sustainability Academy. Thanks to the generous support from the Kenan Institute for Engineering, Technology & Science, NC State University’s Sustainability Fund and the R.L. Rabb Science and Society Symposia Endowment, there is no cost to attend the Fall Symposium. Join us for engaging speakers, panel discussions, networking opportunities, the Innovation Showcase and the new Student Poster Contest. Here is how you can participate: Register to attend the symposium.Complete our registration form to do one or more of the following:Host a table at the Innovation Showcase on Wednesday, Oct. 7, between 5:15 and 7 p.m.Attend the Climate Communications Workshop on Thursday, Oct. 8, between 9 and 10:30 a.m.Present at the poster contest on Thursday, Oct. 8, between 5:15 and 7 p.m.

events.name: Hallowed Places Tour
events.description: NC State has recognized 10 irreplaceable buildings, landscapes and natural settings on its Raleigh campus that have accrued significant meaning over time to students, faculty, staff and alumni. We call them Hallowed Places. Take a tour of the seven sites within walking distance of the Memorial Tower and learn about all 10 spots on this tour led by University Communications and Marketing writer, editor and Hallowed Places expert, Tim Peeler (’87). Along the way, we’ll talk about university folklore, icons and legends, as well as the hallowed history of the ground that lies between the tunnels and under the bricks of North Carolina’s largest university. events.description: Filmmaker Dong Jing, director of No English In America and recipient of the best documentary film award at the 2025 Lowell Film Festival, will show students that filmmaking does not have to begin with professional equipment, extensive technical knowledge or a large production team. It can begin simply, for example, with a story that you want to tell. Through a film screening, a conversation with the filmmaker and an audience Q&A, students will gain a practical understanding of how a film develops from an initial idea into a complete work. Jing's central message will be: If you have a story you want to tell, start making it. Filmmaking is more accessible than you may think.
